title: India Bans Export of Lithium-Ion Battery Black Mass With Immediate Effect
excerpt: The Directorate General of Foreign Trade has changed the export status of lithium-ion battery black mass from 'Free' to 'Prohibited' with immediate effect, keeping the mineral-rich recycling material at home for India's battery and electric-vehicle supply chain.
body:
• India has banned the export of lithium-ion battery black mass, changing its export status from "Free" to "Prohibited" with immediate effect, until further orders.
  • The ban, under ITC (HS) Code 85491400, covers unsorted waste and scrap of primary cells, batteries and electric accumulators not containing lead, cadmium or mercury.
  • Black mass is the powder recovered by shredding used lithium-ion batteries; it contains metals such as lithium, cobalt, nickel and manganese.
  • The government said the move ensures greater domestic availability of the material, a secondary source of inputs for battery manufacturing and energy storage.

The Indian government has banned the export of lithium-ion battery black mass, a recycled battery material containing metals such as lithium, cobalt, nickel and manganese, by changing its export status from "Free" to "Prohibited" with immediate effect, Reuters reported.

The Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT), under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, issued the amendment in Notification No. 49/2026-27. It covers the category classified under ITC (HS) Code 85491400: waste and scrap of primary cells, primary batteries and electric accumulators, and spent cells and batteries, unsorted and not containing lead, cadmium or mercury. The notification states that this category includes lithium-ion battery black mass.

What Black Mass Is, and Why It Matters

Black mass is a powder-like material obtained by shredding and processing used lithium-ion batteries. Because it concentrates the metals from spent batteries, it serves as a secondary source of inputs used in battery manufacturing, energy storage and other advanced industrial applications — which is why governments treat it as a strategic material rather than ordinary scrap.

The DGFT said the prohibition is intended to ensure greater domestic availability of the mineral-rich material. In practice, it means Indian recyclers can no longer ship black mass to processors overseas; the material has to be processed at home, supporting India's electric-vehicle supply-chain ambitions.

The Policy Around It

The amendment was made under the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992, and the Foreign Trade Policy, 2023. The transitional arrangement under Paragraph 1.05 of the Foreign Trade Policy, 2023 will apply, the notification said — the provision that governs shipments already in the pipeline when a policy changes.

The ban follows the Union Cabinet's approval of a Rs 2,814 crore capital-support scheme to promote domestic critical mineral processing, according to reporting on the notification, and a Rs 1,500 crore incentive scheme announced in September 2026 to encourage recycling of critical minerals from secondary sources, including spent batteries and electronic waste.

Read together, the sequence is a supply-chain strategy: pay to build domestic processing capacity, incentivise recycling, and then stop the feedstock leaving the country. For India's battery makers, the test is whether domestic processors can absorb the black mass that exporters previously sold abroad — at prices that keep recycling viable now that the overseas buyer is off the table.
